newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan investors flock to high-risk "plain vanilla".
newsitem.headline: Japan investors flock to high-risk "plain vanilla".

text.p: Heartened by recent profits they reaped from dual currency bonds, Japan"s retail investors are now charting the more dangerous territory of foreign bond investments, underwriting sources said on Monday.

"Dual currency bonds are for beginners," one underwriter, who declined to be named, said. "But more ordinary folks are increasingly taking risks by buying straight foreign bonds, like sterling-based ones."

As domestic interest rates crawl at rock-bottom levels, private investors have shifted funds from bank deposits and postal savings into higher risk foreign straight bonds, known by the deceptively innocent name of "plain vanilla".

The sources said many private investors profited from their recent dual currency investments after the yen"s sharp drop, and this has given them a buffer for stepping up their investments in the higher risk, higher return variety.
"With the return they made from dual currency, private investors are buying higher yielding bonds," said Masaru Hamazaki, deputy manager at Yamaichi Research Institute.
"At first, people had doubts about foreign bond investment, but they have become more comfortable, especially after finding out how profitable it can be," he said.
"In the past, retail investors rarely made a profit out of foreign bond investments because of the yen"s appreciation," one senior underwriter at a Japanese brokerage said.
"Given the ongoing downward trend in the yen and the slump in the Japanese stock market, where else besides foreign bonds can you receive a reasonable return?" he said.

The boom in foreign straight bonds is expected to continue, with a shift toward pound-based bonds and U.S. dollar-based bonds rather than the Australian dollar after a series of credit-easings there last year.

The issuing volume for yen/Australian dollar dual currency samurais dropped sharply this year. Among the 12 dual samurais -- worth a total of about 350 billion yen -- issued since January, 10 tranches were yen/U.S. dollar and one each was in yen/Australian dollar and yen/New Zealand dollar, underwriters said.
In 1996, a record of 2.4 trillion yen worth of dual currency samurais were issued, with about 70 to 80 percent of them in yen/Australian dollar, underwriters said.
With investors" appetite for high-yielding instruments growing, many domestic securities houses are trying to lure them with offerings of sterling-based bonds.
Japanese securities houses have already lead-managed more than 1.0 billion pounds (200 billion yen) worth of sterling-based bonds since the start of the year, underwriters said.
Yamaichi Securities said that its branch offices have been inundated with orders for sterling bonds from their customers.

"We"ve managed to sell out 50 billion yen (250 million sterling) worth of Euro sterling bonds in just three days since subscription," said Shingo Ishizaki, deputy general manager of the market planning department at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
Yamaichi lead-managed 250 million pounds worth of Eurobonds issued by the International Financial Corp earlier this month.
The dual samurais, meanwhile, are still enjoying strong demand, with a total of nearly 250 billion yen offered in February.
Careful investors are buying them to protect themselves from currency risks as the coupons are received in yen, underwriters said.
The coupon rate of straight foreign bonds with similar maturities and credit rating are usually set at higher levels than dual currency bonds.
